subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which erosion process involves the sheer force of moving water hitting and forcing air into cracks in the river bed and banks?
questions.explain: Hydraulic action is the force of the water itself compressing air in cracks and dislodging material.

questions.q: Which transportation process describes small stones and pebbles bouncing along the river bed?
questions.explain: Saltation is the bouncing or hopping of small particles along the river bed.

questions.q: The wearing away of the river bed and banks by the load the river carries is known as?
questions.explain: Abrasion (corrasion) is when the transported load scrapes and grinds against the bed and banks.

questions.q: By which process do transported rocks collide with one another, becoming smaller, smoother and rounder?
questions.explain: Attrition is the collision of load particles that reduces them to smaller, rounded fragments.

questions.q: A steep drop in the river's long profile formed where a band of hard rock overlies softer rock is a?
questions.explain: A waterfall forms where resistant rock overlies softer rock that is eroded more quickly.

questions.q: A crescent-shaped lake left behind when a meander loop is cut off from the main channel is a?
questions.explain: An ox-bow lake forms when erosion breaks through the neck of a meander and the loop is sealed off by deposition.

questions.q: The wide, flat area of land either side of a river that is covered when the river floods is called the?
questions.explain: The floodplain is the flat valley floor built up by deposition of alluvium during floods.

questions.q: Building concrete flood walls and channelising a river to contain high flows is an example of?
questions.explain: Hard engineering uses artificial structures such as walls and channels to control the river.

questions.q: Why does a river deposit its load when its velocity decreases?
options: It loses energy and can no longer transport the material
It gains energy and erodes more material
The gradient of the channel increases
questions.explain: A fall in velocity reduces the river's energy, so it drops the largest particles first.

questions.q: Why does a waterfall gradually retreat upstream to leave a gorge?
options: Undercutting of the soft rock causes the overhanging hard rock to collapse repeatedly
Deposition builds up the channel bed over time
The river's velocity falls at the base of the fall
Solution dissolves the hard rock cap first
questions.explain: Erosion of the softer rock undercuts the hard cap rock, which collapses and the process repeats, cutting a gorge.

questions.q: Why is erosion greatest on the outside bend of a meander?
options: Water flows faster and deeper, causing lateral erosion
Water flows slower, so deposition dominates
questions.explain: Faster, deeper flow on the outer bank increases erosion, forming a river cliff.

questions.q: How are natural levées formed along a river?
options: Coarser sediment is deposited first at the channel edges during floods, building up raised banks
The river erodes downwards to leave raised banks
Meanders migrate to leave ridges of sediment
Distributaries deposit sediment out at sea
questions.explain: When a river floods, the heaviest material is dropped closest to the channel, raising the banks over time.

questions.q: How does the long profile of a river typically change from source to mouth?
options: The gradient becomes gentler towards the mouth
The gradient becomes steeper towards the mouth
The river narrows towards the mouth
questions.explain: The long profile is concave, steep near the source and progressively flatter towards the mouth.

questions.q: Why does deforestation within a drainage basin increase the risk of flooding?
options: Less interception means more rapid surface runoff reaches the river
More water is stored in the soil, raising the water table
Rainfall totals in the basin increase
Infiltration rates increase across the basin
questions.explain: Removing trees reduces interception and infiltration, so water reaches the channel faster, raising flood risk.

questions.q: Why does urbanisation with concrete and tarmac surfaces increase flood risk?
options: Impermeable surfaces reduce infiltration and increase surface runoff
They raise infiltration rates into the ground
They reduce the discharge of nearby rivers
questions.explain: Impermeable urban surfaces prevent water soaking in, so runoff reaches rivers quickly via drains.

questions.q: A town wants a low-cost, environmentally sustainable way to reduce flood risk in its upper catchment. Which method best fits?
questions.explain: Afforestation is a soft-engineering method that increases interception and infiltration, reducing runoff at low cost.

questions.q: A river channel has a cross-sectional area of 10 m² and a velocity of 2 m/s. What is its discharge?
A river reaches the sea in a sheltered area with little tidal movement and splits into many distributaries as it deposits its load. Which landform is forming?
questions.explain: Deltas form where a river deposits large amounts of sediment at its mouth faster than the sea can remove it, splitting into distributaries.

questions.q: Following weeks of rain, the soil in a basin is fully saturated and further heavy rain falls. Why does flood risk rise sharply?
options: Saturated soil prevents further infiltration, so almost all rainfall becomes surface runoff
Saturated soil increases infiltration, storing more water
questions.explain: Once the soil is saturated, water cannot infiltrate, so additional rainfall flows rapidly overland into the river.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Geography (4GE1) specification; River Environments
